title: Pancreatic Cancer Vaccine Stimulates Immune Response in 90 Percent of High-Risk Patients in Early Trial
excerpt: An off-the-shelf vaccine targeting KRAS mutations showed durable T-cell responses and no cancer recurrence after 16.5 months of follow-up, raising hopes for one of the deadliest cancers.
body:
• An experimental vaccine targeting KRAS gene mutations stimulated significant immune responses in 18 of 20 participants (90 percent) who are at high risk of developing pancreatic cancer.
  • After a median follow-up of 16.5 months, none of the participants developed pancreatic cancer, and vaccine-induced T-cell clones remained detectable for up to two years.
  • A separate personalized mRNA vaccine trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering showed that nearly 90 percent of patients whose immune systems responded were still alive up to six years after treatment — compared to the disease's overall five-year survival rate of about 13 percent.
  • Both vaccines are in early-stage clinical trials and are not yet available outside research settings.

Two experimental vaccines for pancreatic cancer have delivered striking results in early clinical trials, offering rare optimism for a disease that kills more than 50,000 Americans each year and carries a five-year survival rate of just 13 percent.

The Prevention Vaccine

In a phase 1 trial targeting individuals at high risk of developing pancreatic cancer, researchers found that 18 of 20 participants — 90 percent — developed a significant immune response to a vaccine targeting KRAS gene mutations. KRAS mutations drive about 90 percent of pancreatic cancers and are among the most common genetic drivers of solid tumors.

Participants experienced a median 18.2-fold increase in mutant KRAS-specific T-cell responses. The vaccine generated both CD4-positive helper T cells and CD8-positive killer T cells, and produced memory T cells that remained detectable for up to two years after vaccination.

"Seven of those eight "vaccine responders" were still alive at the six-year mark."

"Seven of those eight "vaccine responders" were still alive at the six-year mark."

After a median follow-up of 16.5 months, none of the participants developed pancreatic cancer or a high-risk lesion requiring surgical removal. Five of the 20 participants experienced complete disappearance of small pancreatic cysts on follow-up imaging, while three others showed partial regression.

The vaccine was well-tolerated. All side effects were mild to moderate — primarily injection-site reactions, fatigue, chills, and flu-like symptoms that resolved without treatment.

The Treatment Vaccine

A separate trial led by Dr. Vinod Balachandran at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center has produced equally compelling results using a personalized mRNA vaccine developed by BioNTech and Genentech. Follow-up data presented at the 2026 American Association for Cancer Research annual meeting showed that nearly 90 percent of patients who generated an immune response to the vaccine were still alive up to six years after surgery.

"These early results show this new immunotherapy approach has the potential to make a difference for one of the deadliest cancers."

— Dr. Vinod Balachandran, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

The phase 1 trial included 16 patients with operable pancreatic cancer. Eight showed positive immune responses after receiving the vaccine following surgery, along with immunotherapy drugs and chemotherapy. Seven of those eight "vaccine responders" were still alive at the six-year mark. Only two of the eight non-responders survived.

Off-the-Shelf vs. Personalized

The two approaches represent different strategies. The KRAS-targeting vaccine, called ELI-002 2P and developed by Elicio Therapeutics, is an "off-the-shelf" product designed to work across patients without customization. It uses amphiphile technology to shuttle antigens directly to lymph nodes, where immune responses are activated. The MSK vaccine is individualized for each patient based on their tumor's specific mutations.

Both approaches share a common insight: priming the immune system to recognize cancer-associated mutations before or shortly after they cause disease, rather than waiting until the cancer has spread.

What's Next

Researchers caution that both studies are early-stage and designed primarily to evaluate safety and immune responses, not to definitively prove that the vaccines prevent cancer. The small sample sizes and relatively short follow-up periods limit conclusions about long-term clinical efficacy. Larger randomized trials are needed before either vaccine could reach patients outside of clinical research settings. But for a disease where 90 percent of patients are diagnosed too late for surgery, the prospect of a preventive vaccine represents a fundamental shift in approach.
